claims.text: The target materials are nanocrystalline HEA components produced by sputtering or powder metallurgy.
Untreated HEA surfaces experience direct metal-to-metal contact and lack a pre-formed lubricious oxide film.
Controlled post-synthesis thermal oxidation at a controlled oxygen partial pressure will form a thin, adherent spinel-type oxide film on the HEA.
The oxidation treatment will reduce both coefficient of friction and wear rate over a wide service-temperature range.
Related HEA tribology work has tested temperatures from approximately 22 °C to 900 °C.
HEA tribological testing has also been conducted at room temperature and 300 °C under a controlled 1 N load and 0.1 m/s sliding speed.
The treatment produces a continuous, nanometer-scale spinel or related oxide tribofilm on the outermost alloy surface.
The oxide film minimizes direct metal-to-metal contact.
A spinel-like structure gives the film lower shear strength and enables it to act as a solid lubricant.
The oxide film is self-healing and continuously reforms or repairs minor sliding damage.
Self-repair of the oxide film reduces friction and wear across a broad temperature range.
Compared with untreated HEAs, oxidation will lower coefficient of friction by approximately 20–50%.
Compared with untreated HEAs, oxidation will decrease wear rate by at least one order of magnitude.
The predicted improvements will occur at both room and elevated operating temperatures.
Untreated HEAs have higher friction and accelerated abrasive wear because they lack a pre-formed protective film.
The benefits require the oxide film to remain stable, adherent, and self-healing under operating conditions.
An overly thick oxide, extreme oxygen partial pressure, or chemical attack can eliminate the tribological benefits.
